title: Geopolitical Turmoil Fuels Chevron's (NYSE: CVX) Refining Windfall As Quarterly Earnings Crush Wall Street Targets - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Oct 31, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis, Politics Attacks on refineries across Russia and the Middle East sent global diesel prices surging, and Chevron (NYSE: CVX) was among the biggest beneficiaries of the resulting supply disruption. American refiners moved swiftly to fill the gap left by damaged foreign capacity, and Chevron’s plants ran at 98% of capacity while processing a record of just over one million barrels per day. The result was a refining profit figure that few analysts anticipated, with that segment alone generating $3.59 billion compared with just $638 million during the same period a year earlier. Overall downstream operations earned $4.93 billion for the quarter, more than four times the $1.14 billion the division produced twelve months prior. Those refining gains combined with stronger crude prices to lift Chevron’s total quarterly profit to $9.9 billion, roughly triple what the company earned in the year-ago period. Earnings per share came in at $5.06, a dramatic improvement from $1.82 a year earlier, while adjusted earnings of $5.28 per share cleared Wall Street’s consensus estimate of $4.89 with room to spare. Higher crude prices added further fuel to the quarter’s strong performance, with Brent averaging $97 per barrel against $69 during the comparable period, pushing upstream earnings to $5.7 billion from $3.3 billion. The surge in profitability translated directly into cash generation, with Chevron producing $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow, up sharply from $4.9 billion in free cash flow a year earlier. Management deployed that capital on multiple fronts, cutting total debt by $3.5 billion during the quarter while sustaining share repurchases at $2.5 billion. Looking beyond North America, Chevron disclosed plans for significant additional investment in Venezuela, where its joint ventures are expected to commit $7 billion over the coming five years. Investors responded positively to the results, sending Chevron shares approximately 2% higher in premarket trading following the earnings release. The quarter underscores how geopolitical instability, far from being a uniform drag on energy companies, can generate extraordinary windfalls for integrated oil majors with large and efficiently run refining operations. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

Bonner said fourth-quarter spending is expected to rise from third-quarter levels, though Chevron still expects to finish 2026 at the low end of its annual capital-spending guidance. Management said it does not plan to change its capital-allocation framework despite its strengthened balance sheet. Bonner reiterated Chevron's priorities of growing its dividend, investing efficiently, maintaining a strong balance sheet and repurchasing shares through the cycle. The company maintained its buyback range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. → Johnson Controls Beats the Heat in AI Data Centers "We're on track with our 2030 plan that we guided in the investor day," Bonner said, adding that Chevron expects to provide more detail on its 2027 capital program following a December board meeting. Chevron outlined plans to increase gross production from its three Venezuelan joint ventures to roughly 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, from about 300,000 barrels per day expected by year-end. Wirth said the program would rely on primary recovery, be self-funding and could extend further into the 2030s. The company expects total costs in Venezuela to be below $20 per barrel, including capital and operating costs. Bonner said Chevron does not anticipate major new infrastructure spending to support the production increase, describing the program as a "factory-like operation" that could become more efficient over time. Wirth said revised fiscal terms have made Venezuela more competitive in Chevron's portfolio and immediately accretive to free cash flow. Chevron markets all crude produced from the three ventures, with most volumes going to U.S. refineries including Pascagoula and El Segundo. Addressing risk in the country, Wirth cited contract provisions including stability clauses and international arbitration. He also said Chevron's control of crude marketing and revenue flows, along with its intention to fund development through venture-generated cash flow, differentiates the current arrangement from prior structures. Elsewhere, Chevron said it continues negotiations on an extension of its Tengizchevroil, or TCO, concession in Kazakhstan. Wirth said discussions have progressed over more than a year, with technical, commercial and legal teams narrowing the issues to "fundamental core issues." He said the company sees no red flags but did not offer a timeline for an agreement. Chevron reported a quarterly natural-gas production record of more than 9 billion cubic feet per day, led by Australia and the Eastern Mediterranean. The company also cited record quarterly deepwater production in the U.S. Gulf of America, its sixth consecutive quarter of Permian output above 1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, and TCO operations near full rates in recent months. Vice Chairman Mark Nelson said debottlenecking projects have added more than 85,000 barrels per day of upstream capacity. Chevron increased capacity at TCO's third-generation plant by 20%, lifting total processing capacity to slightly above 1 million barrels per day. Capacity additions at Ballymore and Anchor also supported Gulf of America output. In refining, Chevron achieved record quarterly U.S. crude throughput. Nelson said a proprietary catalyst deployed at its largest U.S. refineries raised distillate yields by more than 10%. U.S. distillate yield reached 46% in the third quarter, while Pascagoula achieved a diesel-production record over at least the past three to four years, according to Nelson. The company accelerated debottlenecking at its Pasadena refinery to raise capacity by about 15% at what Nelson called nominal cost. Chevron also expects to increase Pascagoula refining capacity by another 7% by 2030. In the Bakken, Chevron expects a restructuring of Hess Midstream contracts to reduce tariffs by 50%, improve upstream returns, expand economic inventory and provide greater operating flexibility. The company plans to reduce its rig count from three to two by year-end while sustaining 180,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Chevron expects the transaction to close at the end of the fourth quarter and record a one-time, non-cash after-tax loss of $3 billion to $4 billion as a special item related to deconsolidation accounting. Its ScoutAI tool is being deployed across 10 new basins to conduct basin assessments in hours rather than weeks. The company reported 15 infrastructure-led discoveries over two years, with a 40% success rate, and plans to increase exploration spending by 50% compared with 2025. The oil giant's profit nearly tripled from the year-ago period, while free cash flow more than doubled. Those impressive results highlight Chevron's ability to generate enormous amounts of cash when energy markets are favorable. U.S. downstream earnings rocketed more than 450% to almost $3.6 billion, while earnings from its international downstream operations jumped more than 150% to $1.3 billion. content: U.S. energy supermajor Chevron Corporation CVX reported adjusted third-quarter 2026 earnings per share of $5.28, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.78. The bottom line surged 185.4% from the year-ago adjusted profit of $1.85 per share. The integrated energy giant generated revenues of $67.8 billion, exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $60.5 billion by 12.1%. Revenues increased 36.3% year over year. Chevron's worldwide net oil-equivalent production averaged 3,980 thousand barrels of oil-equivalent per day (MBOE/d), declining 2.6% from 4,086 MBOE/d a year earlier. Lower entitlements resulting from higher commodity prices and disruptions related to the Middle East conflict weighed on volumes. The upstream segment recorded earnings of $5.7 billion, increasing 72.6% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago quarter. Higher liquids realizations and lower operating costs supported profitability despite reduced overall production. Its non-GAAP profit of $5.28 per share was 8.5% above analysts' consensus estimates. For more on Chevron, read our full research report. Revenue $67.8 billion vs S&P analysts' consensus estimates of $61.04 billion (36.3% year-on-year growth, 11.1% beat) Adjusted EPS $5.28 vs S&P analysts' consensus estimates of $4.87 (8.5% beat) Operating margin 20.1%, up from 11.6% in the same quarter last year Free cash flow margin 17.7%, up from 9.9% in the same quarter last year Oil production in line with the same quarter last year "We're reinvesting to bring more energy to a supply-constrained market," Wirth continued. In Venezuela, Chevron's joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of generating low-cost, high-return and long-duration production growth. In the United States, the company signed agreements to reduce Bakken midstream costs by approximately 50 percent, strengthening the asset's competitiveness. "Building on our performance this quarter, we're focused on delivering the reliable energy the world needs today, while positioning Chevron for the future," Wirth concluded. A company's long-term performance can give signals about its business quality. Even a bad business, especially in a cyclical industry, can perform well for a year or so, but a top-tier one should exhibit resilience through cycles. Over the last five years, Chevron grew its revenue at a decent 10.8% compounded annual growth rate. Its growth was slightly above the average energy upstream and integrated energy company and shows its offerings resonate with customers. Even a long stretch in energy can be shaped by a single commodity cycle, so extending the view to ten years adds another perspective and reveals which companies are built to grow regardless of the pricing regime. Chevron's annualized revenue growth of 7.6% over the last ten years is below its five-year trend, but the results were still good. While looking at revenue is important, it can also introduce noise around commodity prices and M&A. Analyzing production, on the other hand, highlights what is happening inside the asset base and whether the economic footprint of a company is expanding. Over the last two years, Chevron's oil production averaged 14.1% year-on-year growth while its natural gas production averaged 14.4% year-on-year growth. This quarter, Chevron reported strong year-on-year revenue growth of 36.3%, and its $67.8 billion of revenue exceeded Wall Street's consensus estimates by 11.1%. Chevron also reported modest year-on-year oil production growth of 0.1%. Adjusted EBITDA margin strips out accounting distortions tied to depletion and historical drilling spend, providing a clearer view of the cash-generating power of the underlying asset base before financing and reinvestment decisions. Chevron was profitable over the last five years but held back by its large cost base. Its average EBITDA margin of 25.3% was weak for an upstream and integrated energy business. On the positive side, Chevron's EBITDA margin rose by 1.2 percentage points over the last year, as its revenue growth gave it operating leverage. This quarter, Chevron generated an EBITDA margin of 29.3%, up 5.9 percentage points year on year. The increase was a positive sign of greater efficiency. Adjusted EBITDA fell short of Wall Street's consensus estimates. Adjusted EBITDA shows how profitable a company's existing "rock" is before financing and reinvestment, while free cash flow shows how much value remains after paying to replace those wells. Because production declines over time, strong EBITDA can coexist with weak FCF if drilling is expensive or declines are steep. FCF therefore captures both operating efficiency and the cost of sustaining production. Chevron has shown strong cash profitability, giving it the option to reinvest or return capital to investors. The company's free cash flow margin averaged 11.6% over the last five years, better than the broader energy upstream and integrated energy sector. The level of free cash flow is important, but its durability across cycles is just as critical. Consistent margins are far more valuable than volatile swings driven by commodity prices. Chevron's ratio of quarterly free cash flow volatility to WTI crude price volatility over the past five years was 4.9 (lower is better), indicating strong insulation from commodity swings. This stability supports capital access in downturns and positions Chevron to act as a consolidator when weaker peers are forced to retrench. Why use free cash flow to assess stability against commodity prices rather than compare Chevron's revenue or EBITDA to WTI? What ultimately matters is not how much revenue or profit a company earns when prices are high but how much cash it can generate when prices are low. Free cash flow is the superior metric because it captures hedging effectiveness, growth and maintenance capex and management behavior during good times and bad. Chevron's free cash flow totaled $12 billion in Q3, equivalent to a 17.7% margin. This was a positive result, as its margin was 7.8 percentage points higher than in the same quarter last year. Its cash profitability was also above its five-year level. Chevron delivered a solid quarter, with revenue well ahead of analysts' consensus estimates and EPS also topping Wall Street's estimates. title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars - CNBC
content:
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices. Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday. The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence. ExxonMobil’s profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street’s expectations. “Refining capacity is very tight today,” Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. “Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand.” U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September. Chevron’s net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street’s expectations of $4.89. “The system is under stress,” Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. “We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile.” Here’s what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon “were making too much money based on a shortage.” The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Profits from Chevron’s refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period. Chevron’s U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said. Exxon’s refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business’ earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025. Exxon’s Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced “record volumes of diesel” in the quarter, Woods said. Chevron’s oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year.
